 This guide is for people powering a tiny house they actually live in, on a trailer or on a foundation. That job is not a bigger version of camping. The battery gets cycled every day for years, the loads are small but never stop, and every inch the unit occupies is an inch the house does not get back. We compared four expandable power stations on the specifications that decide those three things: capacity against a stated daily budget, expansion ceiling, rated cycle life, solar input and physical size. We did not test any of these units, and each review says exactly what its recommendation is based on. What you get here is one daily energy budget written out in full, every capacity converted into days of autonomy, cycle ratings converted into years at a tiny-house duty cycle, and watt-hours per cubic foot for the bay you are about to frame.
 What is the best solar generator for a tiny house?
 The BLUETTI AC200L suits most tiny houses because its 1200W solar ceiling accepts far more panel than a typical daily budget needs, which is what carries you through short winter days, and it expands to 8192Wh. If the battery has to hide on a shallow shelf, the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus is only 8 inches deep.
 Key takeaways
 Size a tiny house from its daily watt-hour budget and continuous average draw, not from peak wattage
 A published solar input ceiling is a design constraint, because you cannot bolt on more panel than the unit will accept
 Cycle ratings assume one full cycle a day, so a 1024Wh pack on a 1.7kWh budget burns through them in about 60% of the advertised years
 Buying capacity you do not yet need slows battery ageing, because shallow cycles count proportionally
 Watt-hours per cubic foot matters more than pounds when you are framing a permanent battery bay

 A tiny house is not a camping trip with a smaller tent. The battery gets cycled
every single day, forever, and the thing that decides whether that works is not
capacity. It is whether you can put the energy back in.
 Why solar input ceiling is the number that matters here # 
 Take a modest full-time tiny-house day: a 12V compressor fridge averaging 45W
across its duty cycle, five hours of LED lighting at 20W, a router drawing 10W
around the clock, four hours of laptop and phone charging at 60W, and a water
pump running twelve minutes. That is 1,672Wh, call it 1.7kWh, and it averages
about 70W continuously.
 To replace 1,672Wh in a 4.5 peak-sun-hour day you need roughly 372W of panel
producing at nameplate. Derate to a realistic 75% for heat, wiring and angle and
you are looking for about 500W of array.
 The AC200L accepts 1200W. That is 2.4 times what the budget needs, and the
headroom is the point. On a December day that delivers two usable hours instead
of four and a half, an oversized array is the only thing that keeps the pack
level. A unit capped at 400W simply cannot use the extra panel you bolt on.
 What 2048Wh buys before the sun comes back # 
 At the 70W continuous average above, 2048Wh runs for 29 hours. Against the full
daily budget it is 1.2 days. That is the practical difference between this and
the 1024Wh units here: a fully overcast day does not force you to choose between
the fridge and the lights.
 Expanded to 8192Wh, the same budget gives about 4.9 days of autonomy, which
covers a genuine winter weather system rather than one bad afternoon.
 Where it costs you # 
 Sixty-one pounds in a house where every pound rides on a trailer axle is a real
decision, and it is not a unit you reposition on a whim. Build the bay, vent it,
and accept that it lives there.
 The recharge figure needs reading carefully too. Refilling 1,638Wh in 45 minutes
means pulling about 2,185W. From a house hookup, fine. From the 2000W inverter
generator most tiny-house owners actually own, that rate is not available, and
your refill takes proportionally longer.
 Who should choose something else # 
 If the house will spend its winters plugged into shore power or topped up from a
generator, you are paying for solar headroom you will never use. The OUPES Mega 1
reaches 80% in 36 minutes on about 1,365W of input, a rate a 2000W inverter
generator can actually deliver, which is not true of the 2,185W this unit’s
45-minute figure assumes. If floor area is the binding constraint rather than
sun, the DELTA 3 Plus takes about 30% less of it.

 Every other specification in this category is negotiable in a tiny house. Floor
area is not. The DELTA 3 Plus wins here because of a dimension most buying guides
never print.
 Eight inches of depth changes where it can live # 
 At 16 x 8 x 11 in, this unit occupies 128 square inches of floor. The AC200L
occupies 181.5. That is roughly 30% less of the scarcest resource in the
building, and the 8-inch depth is the part that matters most: it clears a shallow
shelf, a stair riser cavity or an under-counter run that the AC200L’s 11-inch
depth simply will not enter.
 Per cubic foot it holds about 1,257Wh, which is not the best figure here. But
volume is not what constrains a tiny house. Where the box can physically go is.
 The cycle-life arithmetic, done honestly # 
 A 4,000-cycle rating sounds like a lifetime, and manufacturers let you assume it
means eleven years. That assumption only holds at one full cycle a day.
 Run this unit alone against the 1.7kWh daily budget used throughout this guide
and you are drawing 1,672Wh from a 1,024Wh pack, which is about 1.63 equivalent
full cycles every day. Four thousand cycles at that rate is roughly 2,450 days,
or 6.7 years.
 Now add the expansion pack. At 5kWh the same daily draw is about a third of a
cycle, and the rated cycles stop being the limiting factor at all: calendar
ageing takes over long before you count them out. This is the strongest argument
for buying capacity you do not immediately need, and it applies to every unit
here.
 What it does not do # 
 One thousand and twenty-four watt-hours is 14.6 hours at a 70W continuous draw.
A full-time tiny house does not fit inside that, and pretending otherwise is how
people end up rationing lights in February. Treat the expansion battery as part
of the purchase, not an upgrade.
 The other gap is planning. There is no published solar input ceiling in the
specification set we compared, so if your build starts with an array size and
works backwards, you cannot do that arithmetic against this unit. The AC200L
gives you a number to design against.
 Who should choose something else # 
 If the unit is going in an open bay where depth does not matter, the AC200L
carries twice the energy and a solar ceiling you can plan around. If you charge
mainly from a small generator, the OUPES Mega 1 puts the same 819Wh back in 36
minutes instead of 40, and pairs it with a 2000W inverter.

 Most tiny houses are not purely solar, whatever the brochure photographs imply.
There is a generator in the trailer box, or a friend’s outlet, or a campground
pedestal for two hours. The question is how much energy you can capture in the
window you actually get.
 What 36 minutes is worth # 
 Eighty percent of 1024Wh is 819Wh. Returning that in 36 minutes means the unit is
averaging roughly 1,365W of input.
 Set that against the daily budget used across this guide, 1,672Wh for a fridge,
lights, a router, device charging and a water pump. Thirty-six minutes of
generator run time covers about 49% of that day.
 Running longer does not scale the way people assume, because the pack itself is
the ceiling. A completely full 1024Wh is 61% of the budget, so no single charging
session covers a tiny-house day outright. The generator has to come back the next
day, or the array has to carry the rest.
 Run AC and solar together and the same 819Wh arrives in 26 minutes. For anyone
who parks somewhere with power for a lunch break, that is the difference between
a useful stop and a token one.
 The inverter is bigger than the box suggests # 
 Two thousand watts continuous from a 27.8 lb unit is not typical, and the 4500W
surge rating is the headline. In a tiny house it changes what the kitchen can be.
A 1500W inverter rules out most induction hobs and makes a shallow-well pump a
gamble. This clears both.
 That capability is why the OUPES appears here rather than higher-capacity units
that stop at 1500W: in a small dwelling the load you cannot start is a bigger
problem than the hour of runtime you do not have.
 Where the arithmetic turns against it # 
 One thousand and twenty-four watt-hours is 14.6 hours at 70W continuous. In a
house that never switches off, that is one night. There is no version of this
unit as a standalone tiny-house battery.
 Expansion fixes the capacity but not the packaging. Two B2 batteries take it to
5120Wh, about three days of autonomy, and they arrive as two more boxes to house,
strap down and ventilate. Plan the bay for three units, not one.
 The larger planning gap is solar. Without a published input ceiling we could
compare, you cannot size a permanent array against this unit with any
confidence. If your build starts with panels on a roof, that is a genuine reason
to look at the AC200L instead.
 Who should choose something else # 
 Full-time solar with no generator points at the AC200L and its 1200W ceiling.
Wanting one box on one shelf points at the DELTA 3 Plus. This unit earns its
place when the charging source is intermittent and the kitchen is electric.

 Tiny houses that were designed rather than assembled are usually 12V houses. The
lights are 12V strips, the roof fan is 12V, the water pump is 12V. Feeding those
from an AC power station means converting DC to AC and back to DC for no reason.
 The port list is the reason it is here # 
 Two DC5521 barrel outputs and a car port cover the three loads a tiny house runs
most hours of most days. Wiring the lighting circuit and the pump to those
outputs skips the inversion step entirely.
 That is not a headline specification and no retailer listing frames it that way,
but in a dwelling where the 12V loads are on for sixteen hours a day and the AC
loads are on for two, it is the port list that decides how the house is wired.
 Densest energy per cubic foot on the shortlist #

works out at about 1,490Wh per cubic foot.

constraint is volume rather than a shallow shelf, this unit gives you the most
stored energy for the cavity you frame.
 In runtime terms, 1548Wh at the 70W continuous draw used throughout this guide is
22 hours. That is very nearly a full day from one box, which none of the 1024Wh
units on this list can claim.

unforgiving. Four hundred watts across 4.5 peak sun hours is 1,800Wh at
nameplate, and about 1,350Wh once you derate 25% for heat, wiring and panel

not help, because the unit will not take it.
 So this is not a solar-primary battery. It is a battery for a house that also
plugs in, runs a generator, or accepts a genuinely smaller daily budget than the

 What to look for before you buy
 Write down your daily budget before you look at a single product # 
 Almost every bad tiny-house battery purchase starts with a capacity number
someone read in a forum. Start with a list instead.
 Here is the budget used throughout this guide. Adjust the numbers to your own
house, but keep the shape.
 12V compressor fridge, averaging 45W across its duty cycle: 1,080Wh
 LED lighting, 20W for five hours: 100Wh
 Router or cellular hotspot, 10W around the clock: 240Wh
 Laptop and phone charging, 60W for four hours: 240Wh
 Water pump, 60W running twelve minutes: 12Wh
 That totals 1,672Wh, or about 1.7kWh. Divided across 24 hours it is a continuous
average of roughly 70W.
 Two things follow. First, the load is modest and relentless, which is the
opposite of the surge-heavy profile a home backup guide optimises for. Second, a
1024Wh unit covers 14.6 hours of it and a 2048Wh unit covers 29.3 hours. Neither
is a week.
 Convert every capacity into days, not hours # 
 Divide capacity by 1,672Wh and the shortlist sorts itself:
 OUPES Mega 1 and DELTA 3 Plus, 1024Wh: 0.6 days
 VTOMAN FlashSpeed 1500, 1548Wh: 0.9 days
 BLUETTI AC200L, 2048Wh: 1.2 days
 Now do the same with the expansion ceilings:
 VTOMAN, 3096Wh: 1.9 days
 DELTA 3 Plus, 5kWh: 3.0 days
 OUPES, 5120Wh: 3.1 days
 AC200L, 8192Wh: 4.9 days
 The gap between those two lists is the real purchase decision. Every unit here is
expandable, and none of them is a complete tiny-house system out of the box.
 The solar input ceiling is a hard limit on your roof # 
 Replacing 1,672Wh in a 4.5 peak-sun-hour day needs about 372W of panel producing
at nameplate. Real panels do not, so derate 25% for heat, wiring losses and a
roof angle that is never ideal, and you need roughly 500W of array.
 That is the summer answer. Winter is what sizes the array, and the standard fix
is to oversize the panels so a two-hour day still puts something back.
 You can only oversize as far as the unit accepts. The AC200L takes 1200W, about
2.4 times the summer requirement, so you can build in that winter margin. The
VTOMAN caps at 400W, which yields roughly 1,350Wh on a good day after derating,
and that is 320Wh short of the budget before a single cloud appears. Bolting on
more panel does not fix it, because the unit will not take the input.
 For the DELTA 3 Plus and the OUPES Mega 1, no solar input ceiling appeared in the
specification set we compared, so we have not sized an array against either one.
 Cycle life only means years if you do the division # 
 Ratings are quoted in cycles, marketing implies years, and the conversion depends
entirely on your budget and your pack size.
 At 1,672Wh a day, a 1024Wh unit runs about 1.63 equivalent full cycles daily. The
DELTA 3 Plus is rated 4,000 cycles to 80%, which sounds like eleven years and is
actually about 6.7. The OUPES is rated 3,500+, roughly 5.9 years at the same
rate. The VTOMAN, at 1548Wh, runs about 1.08 cycles a day, so its 3,000+ rating
is worth roughly 7.6 years. No cycle-life figure was available to us for the
AC200L, so it is absent from this comparison rather than estimated.
 The useful insight is what happens when you expand. Shallow cycles count
proportionally, so a DELTA 3 Plus expanded to 5kWh runs a third of a cycle a day
and stops being limited by cycle count at all. Buying capacity you do not need
today is also buying years.

 Weight matters on a trailer. Volume matters everywhere else.

 EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus: about 1,257Wh
 OUPES Mega 1: about 1,110Wh
 Shape matters as much as volume. The DELTA 3 Plus is 8 inches deep and takes 128
square inches of floor against the AC200L’s 181.5, roughly 30% less, and that
depth is what lets it live under a counter instead of in a dedicated cabinet.
 Measure the cavity before you choose, not after.
 Which one should you buy?
Match your situation on the left to the recommendation on the right.
 Solar will be your only charging source all year
 Recommendation: Buy the BLUETTI AC200L for its 1200W input ceiling, roughly 2.4 times the array a 1.7kWh day needs 
 The battery has to fit under a counter or on a shallow shelf
 Recommendation: Buy the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus, 8 inches deep and 128 square inches of floor 
 You top up from a portable generator or short shore-power stops
 Recommendation: Buy the OUPES Mega 1, which returns 819Wh in 36 minutes, about half a tiny-house day inside a short generator run 
 Your kitchen runs on induction rather than propane
 Recommendation: Buy the OUPES Mega 1 for its 2000W continuous and 4500W surge rating 
 The house is already wired for 12V lights, fans and a water pump
 Recommendation: Buy the VTOMAN FlashSpeed 1500 and feed those circuits from its DC5521 and car outputs 
 You want the most stored energy for the smallest framed cavity
 Recommendation: Buy the VTOMAN FlashSpeed 1500 at about 1490Wh per cubic foot 
 Mistakes buyers make
 Sizing from a camping trip instead of a daily budget, then discovering a 1024Wh unit covers about 14.6 hours of a house that never switches off
 Buying a unit with a low solar input ceiling and then trying to fix a shortfall by adding panel the charge controller will not accept
 Reading a 4,000-cycle rating as eleven years without checking how many cycles a day your own budget actually demands
 Framing a battery bay for the head unit only, then having nowhere to put the expansion batteries that make the system work
 Installing the pack in an uninsulated exterior storage bay, where LiFePO4 cells refuse to charge below freezing
 Choosing a 1500W inverter for a house with an induction hob, which leaves the main cooking appliance unusable
 Our final recommendation
If you want one answer rather than a shortlist, this is the unit that suits the widest
 range of readers in this category.
 Best for solar-first tiny houses 
 BLUETTI AC200L 
 Tiny houses that will run mainly on roof or ground-mount solar all year, where the battery lives in a fixed bay and never needs to be carried anywhere.
 Check price at 
 Questions buyers ask
 How many watt-hours does a tiny house actually use per day?
 Most lean full-time builds land between 1kWh and 3kWh. The budget modelled in this guide is 1,672Wh. Houses with electric cooking, a mini-split or an electric water heater run far higher and are outside what any single unit here covers. Measure your own loads with a plug meter for a week before you buy anything.
 Can a power station replace a wired battery bank and inverter?
 For a modest tiny house, yes, and it saves you a charge controller, an inverter and the wiring between them. Where it stops working is at high continuous loads or when you want the bank in the 5kWh to 15kWh range, at which point a wired system costs less per watt-hour and can be serviced cell by cell.
 Will the battery freeze in an exterior storage bay?
 It will not be damaged by sitting cold, but LiFePO4 cells refuse to accept a charge below freezing to protect themselves. A unit stored in an unheated exterior bay through a northern winter may simply stop charging on the coldest mornings. Keep it inside the insulated envelope if you can.
 Do I need a 30A RV inlet on the house to use one of these?
 No. The AC200L has a 30A RV port that matches an inlet you may already have, but that is a connector convenience, not 30 amps of supply, because a 2400W inverter sits behind it. Every unit here works fine feeding a few circuits or a short run of extension cords instead.
 How long before the battery needs replacing?
 Divide the rated cycles by how many equivalent full cycles a day your budget demands. At 1,672Wh a day the DELTA 3 Plus used alone spends its 4,000 cycles in about 6.7 years, while the same unit expanded to 5kWh cycles so shallowly that calendar ageing, not cycle count, ends its life.
 About the author
 Dan Whitmore 
 Off-grid power editor
 Dan has run cabins, work sites and a travel trailer on battery power since 2016. He writes the load maths and runtime sections at Power Bencher.
 Areas of expertise

None of these units were tested by us, and every review names the sources it relies on.

 By Serhii Dovzhenko , Solar & Energy Storage Specialist · Updated November 3, 2026 · Prices checked October 26, 2026 · Data verification: Adsec.ca
 Quick answer For a typical full-time home, the Sungold Power FR-12K20CP ($9,401) is the best off-grid solar kit: a 12 kW 120/240V inverter, 20.48 kWh of LiFePO4 storage and 7.2 kW of bifacial panels. Cabins can start with the SGR-5KE ($4,304); big homes or farms need the 20 kW SGR-20K32P.
 An off-grid solar kit has to do everything a utility line does: make power by day, store enough for the night and a cloudy spell, and deliver the 120V or 120/240V your appliances expect. Buying the inverter, battery and panels as one matched kit means the charge voltage, battery communication and string voltage already agree.
 The hard part is size: a weekend-cabin kit leaves a family home dark by 9 PM. This guide sorts every complete off-grid kit we have in stock and active on October 26, 2026 by home size, shows the sizing math, and flags the limits that spec sheets bury - 120V-only output, battery current, inverter warranty. Prices are store prices before any promo code; every kit includes an inverter/charger, LiFePO4 batteries and solar panels.

 *Our estimate: array kW x 4 sun hours x 0.75 to allow for wiring, inverter, temperature and dust losses. Listings quote 4 sun hours without losses, about a third higher. Your real number depends on your location and season - northern winters can deliver 2-3 sun hours, the desert Southwest 6 or more.
 Specs come from the manufacturer data on each product page. All eight kits are Sungold Power because that is where our complete in-stock off-grid kits sit today; if you already own panels, battery-and-inverter cores such as the NEXUS 14.3 kWh + EG4 6000XP ($4,544, 6 kW split-phase) are the alternative.
 2. Storage vs daily solar: what each kit can actually support
 An off-grid kit is balanced when the array can refill the battery on an ordinary day and the battery can carry you through the night. The chart shows the pattern. The two small kits store more than their panels make in a day - fine for weekends, not for full-time living. The SGK-8MAX is the opposite: a 5.4 kW array on a 10.24 kWh battery refills quickly even on a short December day, which is why it is popular in northern states. The 12 kW and 20 kW kits are balanced for daily cycling, with roughly a day of storage for the energy they produce.
 3. How to size an off-grid solar kit
 Size four numbers in this order: daily energy, battery, array and inverter. Our Solar Kit Calculator does this from your appliance list and ZIP code; here is the math behind it.
 Step 1: daily energy (kWh per day)
 List what you run and for how long. Typical off-grid profiles:
 Weekend cabin (lights, small fridge, chargers, water pump): 2-5 kWh per day.
 Tiny home or full-time cabin (fridge, washer, Wi-Fi, some mini split use): 6-10 kWh per day.
 Small home with propane cooking and heat (fridge, freezer, well pump, laundry): 10-18 kWh per day.
 All-electric family home : 20-30 kWh per day or more. The average US home uses roughly 28-30 kWh a day on the grid, according to EIA residential averages - off-grid homes usually trim that with propane appliances and efficient heat pumps.
 Step 2: battery (kWh of storage)
 Battery kWh = night-time use / 0.9 (LiFePO4 is commonly run to about 90% depth of discharge) x days of autonomy. Example: a small home using 16 kWh a day burns about 9 kWh between sunset and sunrise. 9 / 0.9 = 10 kWh for one night. Add one cloudy day (16 kWh / 0.9 = about 18 kWh) and you are at about 28 kWh - that is the gap between the 20.48 kWh and 30.72 kWh versions of the same 12 kW kit. A generator input lets you buy less battery and run the generator on the third gray day.
 Step 3: array (kW of panels)
 Array kW = daily kWh / (winter sun hours x 0.75). For the same 16 kWh home at 3 winter sun hours: 16 / (3 x 0.75) = 7.1 kW - the 7.2 kW array in the FR-12K20CP. At 5 sun hours in Arizona the same home needs only 4.3 kW. Size for your worst month, or accept generator hours in December.
 Step 4: inverter (continuous watts, surge and voltage)
 Add up the loads that can run at the same time, then check starting surge. A 1 HP well pump runs at about 1,000-1,500 W but can draw two to three times that for a moment at start; a 3-ton central air unit runs at about 3,000-3,500 W. If anything on the list is 240V - well pump, dryer, range, central air, EV charger - you need split-phase 120/240V output, which rules out the 120V-only SGKT-3PRO, SGM-5K5E and SGR-5KE.
 Step 5: check the battery can feed the inverter
 Battery current = inverter watts / 51.2 V / 0.95. A 12 kW inverter at full load pulls about 247 A; the FR-12K20CP's four CoreX 5 Pro modules have 100 A battery management systems each (400 A combined), so the bank is not the bottleneck. The single 5.12 kWh module in the SGM-5K5E is rated 50 A standard and 100 A maximum, so plan continuous loads around 2.5 kW and treat 5 kW as a short-term ceiling until you add a second module. On the SGR-20K32P, the two PowerMax batteries are rated 150 A continuous each (300 A, about 14.5 kW from battery alone) - the full 20 kW is available when the panels are producing, or by adding a third PowerMax. Our 48V server rack battery guide explains this check.
 Safety note: off-grid kits combine high-voltage PV strings (up to 450-500 V DC open circuit on these inverters) with a 48V battery bank that can deliver thousands of amps into a short. Use the DC breakers and fuses supplied, size cables to the manual, and have a licensed electrician do the AC wiring, grounding and any connection to a building panel. Most jurisdictions require a permit and inspection for a home system. If the house also has a utility connection, use the inverter's transfer function or an approved transfer switch, and never backfeed a home through an outlet.
 4. Price per kWh: where the value is
 Dividing the kit price by the battery kWh it includes is a quick value check (the panels and inverter are in the price too). The 30.72 kWh FR-12K30CP is the best value per kWh at about $428, followed by the SGR-5KE ($467), SGKT-3PRO ($485) and FR-12K20CP ($488). The SGK-8MAX looks expensive by this measure ($682) because a large share of its price is panels - 5.4 kW, more than any kit below the 12 kW class - and the SGM-5K5E ($614) carries the fixed cost of a 5 kW inverter on a single battery module.
 For installed budgets, see our whole-home battery backup cost guide . The federal 25D credit ended for home systems paid for after December 31, 2025 (not tax advice).
 5. Our picks by home size
 Best overall for a full-time home Sungold Power FR-12K20CP - 12 kW, 20.48 kWh, 7.2 kW solar - $9,401
 The FR-12K20CP is the most affordable way into a true whole-home off-grid system. The FR12K-B all-in-one inverter delivers 12,000 W continuous and 24,000 W surge on 120/240V split-phase, so a well pump, mini splits, a dryer and a range all work. Two MPPTs accept up to 13.2 kW of PV, and generator charging, rapid shutdown and breakers are built in. Four CoreX 5 Pro rack batteries (EVE Grade A cells, 100 A BMS, 6,000+ cycles, 10-year warranty) store 20.48 kWh, and sixteen 450 W bifacial N-type panels make about 21-29 kWh on a 4-sun-hour day.
 Pros 12 kW / 24 kW surge split-phase, room for 6 kW more PV, rapid shutdown and breakers built in, expandable
 Cons Inverter warranty listed at 2 years (batteries 10 years); 758 lb kit total ships by freight; indoor (IP20) inverter
 See the FR-12K20CP 
 Best for cloudy winters Sungold Power FR-12K30CP - 12 kW, 30.72 kWh, 9.44 kW solar - $12,150
 Same 12 kW inverter, with six CoreX 5 Pro batteries (30.72 kWh) and sixteen 590 W bifacial panels (9.44 kW). That is 50% more storage and 30% more array than the FR-12K20CP for $3,160 more - the extra half-day of autonomy that matters in the Pacific Northwest, Great Lakes or New England. It is also the lowest cost per kWh of storage in this guide (about $428). Customers also regularly send us price-check links for this kit.
 Pros About 1.5 days of storage for a 20 kWh/day home, best $/kWh here, same expandable platform
 Cons 2-year inverter warranty; 897 lb kit; bigger panels (590 W) need more mounting space per panel
 See the FR-12K30CP 
 Best for small homes with 240V loads Sungold Power SGK-8MAX - 8 kW, 10.24 kWh, 5.4 kW solar - $6,281
 The cheapest kit here with split-phase 120/240V output and a big array. The SPH8048P inverter (UL 1741 by ETL) gives 8,000 W continuous and 16,000 W peak, handles motors up to 5 HP and has two MPPTs for up to 11 kW of PV. Twelve 450 W panels make about 16 kWh on a 4-sun-hour day - more than the 10.24 kWh battery holds, so it refills quickly in short winter days. The battery is four 12V 200Ah LiFePO4 units in series with Bluetooth monitoring and self-heating below 33.8°F.
 Pros 240V well pumps and dryers, large array for the price, self-heating batteries, parallels to 6 inverters
 Cons 10.24 kWh is about one night for a small home; 12V batteries in series rather than 48V rack modules
 See the SGK-8MAX 
 Best value for tiny homes and full-time cabins Sungold Power SGR-5KE - 5 kW, 10.24 kWh, 2.49 kW solar - $4,304
 A balanced 120V kit for a small, efficient home: a 5,000 W inverter (10,000 VA peak, UL 1741 by ETL, built-in Wi-Fi), two SG48100P 5.12 kWh rack batteries (7,000+ cycles) and six 415 W panels. At about $467 per kWh of storage it is the best value below the 12 kW class, and the inverter takes up to 5 kW of PV, so you can double the array later. The limit is voltage: 120V only, so no 240V well pump or dryer.
 Pros 10.24 kWh at under $4,800, Wi-Fi monitoring, room to double the array
 Cons 120V only; 2.49 kW array is light for winter full-time use in the north
 See the SGR-5KE 
 Best for big homes, farms and shops Sungold Power SGR-20K32P - 20 kW, 32.14 kWh, 14.4 kW solar - $14,378
 Two SPH10048P 10 kW inverters in parallel for 20,000 W of split-phase power, two IP65 PowerMax outdoor batteries (32.14 kWh, UL 1973 and UL 9540A, CEC listed, 8,000 cycles, 10-year warranty) and thirty-two 450 W bifacial panels (14.4 kW, about 43-58 kWh a day). As noted in the sizing section, the two batteries alone support about 14.5 kW continuous; add a third PowerMax if you need the full 20 kW at night.
 Pros Most solar and power here, outdoor UL 9540A batteries, 22 kW PV capacity, generator inputs
 Cons 3-year inverter warranty; 1,204 lb kit; battery current limits night-time output to about 14.5 kW
 See the SGR-20K32P

A 24V 3,000 W inverter (6,000 VA peak) with an 80 A MPPT, 40 A AC/generator charging with generator auto-start, and 10 ms UPS transfer; two 24V 100Ah Bluetooth batteries with self-heating and IP65 cases; and four 200 W panels (23.5% efficiency).  7. What to check before you order
 Delivery and handling. The 12 kW and 20 kW kits weigh about 750-1,200 lb and arrive by freight on pallets. Panels in particular are big - about 69 x 45 in each for 450 W modules - so plan for a truck that can reach your site and two people to unload.
 Where the battery lives. LiFePO4 cannot be charged below about 32°F. In an unheated cabin choose a kit with self-heating batteries (SGKT-3PRO, SGK-8MAX) or keep the bank in a conditioned space; the SGR-20K32P's PowerMax batteries are outdoor rated (IP65).
 Mounting. Kits include Z-brackets, not full roof racking or ground-mount frames.
 Warranties. Batteries carry 10-year warranties on the 12 kW and 20 kW kits; inverters are listed at 2-3 years on those kits; panels carry 25-30-year output warranties. Keep the paperwork with the system.
 8. What our customers ask
 Off-grid kit questions reach us by phone, text and email in a few repeating patterns (shared here without any personal details):
 "Is this price right?" Buyers send kit links - including copies of our listings on other sites - to confirm the price. We confirm and send the ecosolarkits.com link.
 "Which 10 kW kit should I get?" Customers often ask us to compare the 10-12 kW Sungold kits. Our usual answer is section 6: 12 kW split-phase for a family home, the 30 kWh version for cloudy winters.
 Sizing. We send the Solar Kit Calculator first, then check the result against the customer's appliance list - especially 240V loads and well pump surge.
 9. Current codes and sales
 Current codes (one code per order): EARLYBF500 ($500 off $8,000+, which covers the 10-20 kW kits), SAVE250 ($250 off $4,000+), ECO100 ($100 off $1,500+) and ECO50 ($50 off, no minimum). ECOBLACK2026 ($150 off $2,000+) is scheduled for November 20 - December 1; our Black Friday solar deals hub tracks every verified price and code.
 10. FAQ
 What is the best off-grid solar kit with battery and inverter?
 For a typical full-time home, the Sungold Power FR-12K20CP ($9,990 on October 26, 2026) is the best all-round off-grid kit: a 12 kW 120/240V split-phase inverter with 24 kW surge, 20.48 kWh of LiFePO4 rack batteries and 7.2 kW of bifacial panels. Smaller homes and cabins can start with the SGR-5KE (5 kW, 10.24 kWh, $4,782), and large homes or farms should look at the 20 kW SGR-20K32P.
 What size off-grid solar kit do I need for my house?
 Start from daily kWh, not house square footage. A weekend cabin uses about 2-5 kWh a day, a tiny home 6-10 kWh, a small home with propane appliances 10-18 kWh, and an all-electric family home 20-30 kWh or more. Then size the array as daily kWh / (winter sun hours x 0.75), the battery as night-time kWh / 0.9 per day of autonomy, and the inverter for loads that run together plus surge.
 How much does a complete off-grid solar system cost in 2026?
 Complete DIY kits with inverter, LiFePO4 battery and panels in stock at Eco Solar Kits range from $2,485 for a 3 kW, 5.12 kWh cabin kit to $15,975 for a 20 kW, 32.14 kWh whole-home kit (prices checked October 26, 2026). Add racking, wiring and a licensed electrician on top. The federal 25D credit no longer applies to home systems paid for after December 31, 2025.
 Can an off-grid solar kit run central air and a well pump?
 Yes, if the kit has 120/240V split-phase output and enough inverter and battery current. A well pump plus 3-ton central air typically needs an 8-12 kW split-phase inverter with surge headroom, such as the SGK-8MAX (16 kW peak) or FR-12K20CP (24 kW surge). 120V-only kits like the SGR-5KE cannot run 240V loads.
 How many days can an off-grid solar battery last without sun?
 Divide usable battery kWh by your daily use. At about 90% usable, the 20.48 kWh FR-12K20CP gives roughly 18 kWh, about one day for a home using 18 kWh a day, while the 30.72 kWh FR-12K30CP gives about 1.5 days. Most full-time homes plan 1-2 days and use a generator for longer cloudy stretches.
 Can I install an off-grid solar kit myself?
 Many owners mount panels themselves, but home systems involve high-voltage PV strings, a high-current 48V bank and AC panel wiring. Most jurisdictions require a permit and inspection, so plan on a licensed electrician for the AC side and any connection to the house, and never backfeed a home through an outlet.
 Is a portable power station a good alternative to an off-grid kit?
 For a weekend cabin, RV or short outages, a large portable power station with panels is simpler. For a home that cycles the battery daily through winter, a 48V kit with 10 kWh or more, a fixed array and split-phase output is cheaper per kWh and easier to expand.
 Want a second opinion? Send us your appliance list and ZIP code and we will match a kit - or compare our best off-grid solar systems , off-grid lithium batteries and off-grid inverters .  Frequently Asked Questions
 Why should I customize my setup here?
 This is a dedicated solar kits for home designed for tiny homes to save you time and effort. Every product is hand-matched for compatibility, so you can get everything you need in one click without endless searching. 
 If you only need a few items, you can also purchase individual products here. The more you buy, the more you save with tiered discounts.
 How many solar panels and batteries do I need to run an AC?
 The number of solar panels and batteries needed to power your AC unit depends on the AC unit’s power consumption, and typical duration of usage. To run a 12000BTU mini-split AC unit (which is commonly used in tiny homes) for several hours per day, we recommend between 1000 and 2000 watts of solar, and between 4 and 8 kilowatt-hours.
 How many solar panels or how much solar power do I need for an off-grid tiny home or small cabin?
 the number of solar panels needed for an off-grid tiny home depends on your daily energy consumption and the capacity of solar panels.
 Can I install a solar system for my off-grid tiny home or small cabin by myself?
 Installing a solar system yourself is possible, but it does require some knowledge of electrical systems. If you feel confident and well-informed, go for it! Installing a Renogy AGM tiny home system requires mounting solar panels, connecting panels to circuit breakers and solar inverter chargers, and then connecting the solar inverter charger to the battery bank. If you have any doubts or want expert guidance, we recommend consulting with a professional or reaching out to our dedicated customer support team. We are here to ensure your solar journey is smooth, successful, and tailored to your specific needs.
 Should I mount the solar panels on the roof or on the ground?
 Roof mounting is more discreet and utilizes existing space. Ground mounting will take up additional space but offers easier access for cleaning/maintenance.
 What is the difference between a 12V and a 48V system?
 The voltage refers to the battery bank's capacity. A 12V system has lower voltage but higher current, which is suitable for small setups. A 48V system has higher voltage and lower current, and experiences lower energy losses in the form of heat (due to reduced current flow), resulting in an overall more efficient system.
 Can this solution be integrated with a grid tied system?
 The answer is yes. This system can be integrated with a grid-tied home and used as a backup/emergency power application. The system is not intended to be tied directly to the grid in such a way that electricity generated by solar may be directly fed back into the grid (such as a fully grid-tied or hybrid solar system is).
 How do I size my electrical system requirements?
 Calculate your daily energy consumption in watt-hours and consider sunlight availability. Choose panels and batteries to meet or exceed your needs.
 How many batteries do I need for an off-grid tiny home or small cabin?
 The number of batteries depends on your daily energy consumption and desired days of autonomy.
 What is the difference between a normal home solar system and an off grid home solar system?
 A normal home solar system is connected to the grid, allowing excess energy to be sent back to the utility. An off-grid solar system operates independently, requiring battery storage for power during periods without sunlight.
 Can my system be expanded in the future?
 Certainly! Yes, your solar system can be expanded in the future to meet increased energy needs. It is designed to allow for the addition of extra components, such as solar panels or batteries, whenever required, providing you with flexibility and adaptability as your energy requirements change over time.

 Best Balcony Solar Kits 2026: Plug-in Solar for US Homes
 This article contains affiliate links: if you buy through them we may earn a commission, at no extra cost to you. Read our affiliate disclosure . 
 It’s a Saturday morning in June. The sun is already hitting the railing of your apartment balcony, the fridge is humming inside, and you’re wondering why all that light can’t knock a few dollars off the power bill. In Germany, millions of people hang a couple of panels on the railing and plug them into an outlet. In the US, balcony solar (also called plug-in solar) is just arriving, state by state.
 The best balcony solar kit for most US homes in a state that allows it is the EcoFlow STREAM Microinverter with two or three rigid panels: 1,200 W at 120 V, UL 1741 listed, 10-year warranty, about $369 before panels. If you want to store midday sun for the evening, the EcoFlow STREAM Ultra adds a 1.92 kWh battery. If your state or utility doesn’t allow plug-in solar yet, a power station charged by balcony panels is legal everywhere because it never connects to your house wiring.
 Below: seven options, five grid-tied plug-in kits and two off-grid alternatives, with their real specs, what each maker says about where they may be used, and an honest estimate of what they produce. We researched and compared them from maker pages, state laws and published data; we did not test them.
 Prices change often. The prices below are what we saw at the maker or a major retailer in October 2026; check the current price before you buy. Several plug-in kits were sold out when we checked. 
 First: is balcony solar legal where you live?
 Check this before you spend anything. A plug-in kit pushes power back through a wall outlet, and in most of the US that still counts as connecting a generator to the grid, which needs your utility’s permission. A few states have passed laws that carve out small plug-in systems:
 Utah (HB 340, in effect since May 7, 2025): devices up to 1,200 W on a standard 120 V outlet, no interconnection agreement, but they must meet the electrical code, be UL (or equivalent lab) certified and must not energize the house during an outage.
 Maryland (HB 1532, signed May 12, 2026): up to 1,200 W; the Public Service Commission says to tell your utility before you install.
 Maine (LD 1730, in effect) and Virginia (HB 395, from January 1, 2027): up to 1,200 W. In Maine, systems over 420 W need a licensed electrician and a utility notice.
 Colorado (HB26-1007, up to 1,920 W) took effect August 12, 2026; its landlord, HOA and sales rules start January 1, 2027. California (SB 868, up to 1,200 W) was signed September 30, 2026 and is not in effect yet. Vermont and Connecticut also have laws in force, and New Hampshire and New Jersey have signed laws not yet in use: see our state-by-state guide .
 New York ‘s SUNNY Act passed the legislature in May 2026 and was waiting for the governor’s signature when we checked.
 Everywhere else, your utility’s interconnection rules apply, and some other states have bills moving. Never plug a solar panel into an outlet against your utility’s rules: ask the utility first. Our is balcony solar legal guide tracks the details state by state, and renters should also check the lease (Virginia’s and Colorado’s laws include renter or HOA protections).
 Our top picks

 The best balcony solar kits
 1. EcoFlow STREAM Microinverter: best overall
 The STREAM Microinverter is the box that turns panel power into 120 V household power and sends it through a standard outlet. It’s rated 1,200 W nominal (10 A), with four pairs of panel terminals on three MPPT trackers, up to 450 W per tracker and 1,200 W of panels in total. It works with third-party panels that use MC4 connectors and run between 16 and 60 V. EcoFlow lists UL 1741 certification with anti-islanding protection, which means it stops sending power when the grid goes down, so it can’t energize lines a utility worker is repairing. It’s NEMA 6 water-resistant and carries a 10-year warranty. EcoFlow’s page says plug-in installation “is currently permitted in Utah, Maryland and Colorado.”
 Good: right at the 1,200 W cap in most state laws; UL 1741 listed; long warranty; add a STREAM Ultra later for storage.
 Watch out: panels are sold separately (the panel bundle was sold out when we checked); no power during an outage on its own; only the states EcoFlow names.
 Best for: homeowners and renters in a plug-in-solar state who want the most output allowed.
 See it at EcoFlow 
 2. EcoFlow STREAM Ultra: best with a battery
 The STREAM Ultra is a 1.92 kWh LFP (lithium iron phosphate) battery with its own grid-tied inverter. It takes up to 2,000 W of panels on four MPPT inputs (500 W each), sends up to 800 W to your outlet on its own or 1,200 W with the STREAM Microinverter, and stacks to 11.52 kWh. EcoFlow rates it for 6,000 cycles to 70% capacity, NEMA 4 water resistance and a 10-year warranty. When the grid fails, EcoFlow says it stops feeding the grid and you can plug appliances straight into its two outlets to run on battery or solar.
 Good: stores midday sun for the evening; doubles as a small outage battery; expandable.
 Watch out: panels extra; same three-state limit as the microinverter; 800 W to the home without the microinverter.
 Best for: people who are out all day and use most of their power after sunset.
 See it at EcoFlow 
 3. US Solar Supplier 810W Plug-In Kit: best complete starter kit
 This Kentucky retailer’s kit is the closest thing in the US to a German-style balcony kit in one box: two Runergy 405 W panels, an APsystems EZ1 microinverter (up to 900 VA at 120 V) and SunModo racking that mounts the panels like an awning. Warranties: 15 years on the panels’ product and 30 years on performance, 10 years on the microinverter, 20 years on the racking. The retailer is clear that the system has to meet local code and be approved for grid connection before use, and it ships by freight.
 Good: panels, inverter and mounting in one order; long warranties; honest about approvals.
 Watch out: sold out (“contact for availability”) when we checked; certification not stated on the page we read; freight delivery.
 Best for: a house or ground-floor deck where you can mount two full-size panels.
 See it at US Solar Supplier 
 4. Zendure SolarFlow Kit: most storage in one kit
 Zendure’s US kit bundles two 410 W rigid panels, the Hub 2000 (up to 1,800 W of solar on two MPPT inputs), two AB2000S LFP batteries (3.84 kWh, expandable to 7.68 kWh), a 900 W microinverter and a smart meter clamp so it can match output to what your home is using. The microinverter is UL 1741 listed with anti-islanding; Zendure says that once the power fails, the microinverters stop. Warranty: 10 years. Zendure gives no state list and asks buyers to “consult the local authorities or professionals.”
 Good: complete kit with storage; smart meter avoids sending power you can’t use to the grid.
 Watch out: sold out and expensive at about $3,932; no backup power during an outage; no state-by-state statement from the maker.
 Best for: a homeowner with yard or deck space who wants storage and is fine waiting for stock.
 See it at Zendure 
 5. Craftstrom 1200W Eco-Line: most panels in a box
 Craftstrom sells a 1,200 W kit of six 200 W panels and three 400 W inverters for about $2,250, and the maker estimates up to 2,160 kWh a year. Read its marketing carefully: the site says the kits are “legal in all 50 states” and need no permits, but only a handful of states have plug-in solar laws, so that claim is the maker’s, not the states’. The page says the inverters are “UL certified” without naming the standard. Ask the company for the UL 1741 listing and your utility for its rules before buying. Its bigger 2 kW + 3 kWh battery kit is above the 1,200 W cap in Utah, Maryland, Maine, Virginia and California and above Colorado’s 1,920 W, so it wouldn’t count as a plug-in device under those laws as written.
 Good: six panels in one order at 1,200 W; in stock when we checked.
 Watch out: legality and certification claims we could not confirm; warranty terms not on the page we read; six panels need a lot of railing.
 Best for: buyers in a plug-in state who have confirmed the listing and have the space.
 See it at Craftstrom 
 6. EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus with balcony panels: best legal-everywhere option
 If your state has no plug-in law, there is a simple workaround that involves no utility at all: hang folding panels on the railing, charge a portable power station, and plug a lamp, laptop, router or fan into the station instead of the wall. The DELTA 3 Plus stores 1,024 Wh of LFP battery, puts out 1,800 W (3,600 W surge), takes up to 1,000 W of solar on two 500 W inputs, and expands to 5 kWh with an extra battery. EcoFlow rates it for 4,000 cycles to 80%, under 30 dB at 600 W, with a 5-year warranty. A good balcony match is one or two EcoFlow NextGen 220 W bifacial panels (IP68, 15.4 lb, about $399 each at EcoFlow).
 Good: no grid connection, so no utility approval; doubles as outage backup; moves with you.
 Watch out: it only powers what you plug into it, so you carry the savings by hand; panels cost extra.
 Best for: renters in states without a plug-in law, and anyone who also wants storm backup.
 Check the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus price on Amazon 
 7. Jackery Solar Generator 1000 v2: off-grid kit with a panel included
 Jackery bundles its Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh LFP, 1,500 W, 3,000 W surge) with a SolarSaga 200 W bifacial panel (IP68, 14.33 lb). The station accepts up to 400 W of solar, and Jackery lists about 7.5 hours of solar charging for this kit in good sun. It’s the easy one-box answer if you want sun-charged power on the balcony without picking parts.
 Good: panel included; legal anywhere; light enough to carry inside.
 Watch out: 400 W solar input limits a second panel; one 200 W panel won’t refill it in a short winter day.
 Best for: small apartments that want a solar-charged backup and a lower electric bill on a few devices.
 Check the Jackery Solar Generator 1000 v2 price on Amazon 
 How much will a balcony kit produce?
 A simple estimate: daily kWh ≈ panel kW × peak sun hours × 0.8. The 0.8 covers heat, wiring, dust, partial shade and inverter losses (NREL’s PVWatts calculator uses 14% system losses before the inverter by default). Most of the continental US gets roughly 4 to 6 peak sun hours a day on average, less in the Northeast and Northwest, more in the Southwest.
 800 W of panels at 4.5 sun hours: about 2.9 kWh a day, or about 1,050 kWh a year.
 1,200 W of panels : about 4.3 kWh a day, or about 1,580 kWh a year.
 Value: at EIA’s 2026 forecast US average of 18.2 cents per kWh, that’s about $190 and $290 a year, but only if your home uses every kWh as it’s made.
 These are our estimates for south-facing, tilted, unshaded panels. Panels hung flat against a railing make noticeably less, east or west faces less again, and a north-facing balcony is rarely worth it. The state laws we read don’t promise payment for power that flows back to the grid, so plan on saving only what your fridge, router and other always-on devices use while the sun is up. That’s why many buyers add a battery: see balcony solar with a battery .
 How to choose a balcony solar kit
 Start with the law and your utility. If your state has a plug-in law, stay under its watt cap (1,200 W in most; 1,920 W in Colorado). If not, ask the utility or choose an off-grid power station kit.
 Insist on a real listing. Look for a microinverter certified to UL 1741 with anti-islanding, named on the maker’s page. Utah’s law requires UL or equivalent lab certification; Colorado’s references UL 3700.
 Measure the space and the sun. Full-size 400 W panels are big and heavy: check the dimensions and weight on the spec sheet against your railing. Count how many fit, which way they face and how many hours of direct sun they get.
 Mount it safely. Panels on a railing catch wind. Use racking made for the job, follow the maker’s instructions and your building’s rules, and never hang anything that could fall on people below.
 Use a dedicated outdoor outlet on a circuit that isn’t overloaded. If you’re unsure, a licensed electrician can check it (Maine’s law requires one above 420 W).
 Don’t expect federal money. The 25D residential clean energy credit ended for systems installed after December 31, 2025. Check your state and utility for rebates.
 Keep exploring
 Our balcony solar guide explains how plug-in solar works in the US. Check whether balcony solar is legal in your state , see how to add storage with balcony solar with a battery , or read solar panels for renters . For bigger panels on a power station, see the best portable solar panels and our portable power stations guide . If you own a roof, solar panels for home covers full systems, and solar energy explains the basics. Browse everything in solar energy .
 Balcony solar kit questions
 Can I buy a balcony solar kit in the US?
 Yes, but the choice is small. EcoFlow sells the STREAM Microinverter and STREAM Ultra, Zendure and US Solar Supplier sell complete kits (both sold out when we checked), and Craftstrom sells multi-panel kits. Most popular European kits, such as Anker’s Solarbank and BLUETTI’s Balco, were not sold in US versions when we checked.
 Is it safe to plug a solar panel into a wall outlet?
 Only with a certified plug-in microinverter that shuts off when the grid goes down, on a circuit that can take it, and where your state or utility allows it. Never wire a panel or a generic inverter to a plug yourself. State laws such as Utah’s require UL or equivalent certification and that the device not energize the house in an outage.
 How much money does a balcony solar kit save?
 Our estimate for an unshaded, south-facing 800 W kit is about 1,050 kWh a year, worth about $190 at the 2026 US average price, if your home uses all of it as it’s made. A vertical or shaded railing makes less, and power sent back to the grid may earn nothing. Treat makers’ payback claims as best cases.
 Do balcony solar kits work during a power outage?
 A plain plug-in kit doesn’t: the microinverter shuts off when the grid fails, by design. A kit with a battery that has its own outlets, like the EcoFlow STREAM Ultra, or a portable power station charged by panels, can keep a few devices running.
 Can renters install balcony solar?
 Often, with care. Get the landlord’s or HOA’s OK unless your state’s law protects you (Virginia’s and Colorado’s include protections), follow the state’s watt cap, and use mounts that leave no damage. An off-grid power station with folding panels needs no one’s permission to use inside your home.
 Written by SolutionEnergy Team
 The SolutionEnergy team researches home and business energy in the U.S. from official sources such as the EIA, the Department of Energy and state utility commissions, and dates every number. We are researchers and writers, not installers, and a person checks every page before it goes live.

The shift accelerated as lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries dropped below $500 per kWh installed in many markets. Homeowners now compare kits by continuous inverter output, battery capacity, and solar input. Our testing approach mimics how an electrician sizes a standby panel: we start with running watts, add surge headroom, then match solar to daily watt-hours. This guide ranks complete systems from big cabin rigs to portable emergency arrays. Before buying, decide whether you need a fixed install or a relocatable unit with how to go off-grid guidance.
 A true off-grid solar kit is more than panels and a power station. It includes a solar charge controller, an inverter, battery storage, and the cables and breakers to connect them safely. Cheap kits omit a transfer switch or use modified sine wave inverters that can damage motor loads. We eliminated any system with no UL or ETL listing, undersized wire, or no low-temperature battery protection. EnergySage recommends checking your local electrical code before a permanent array; some jurisdictions require a rapid shutdown device and a visible disconnect. For whole-home backup versus portable use, our solar battery vs generator 2026 comparison lays out the real tradeoffs.

We scored each kit on surge capacity, battery amp-hour rating, and maximum solar input. For whole-home backup, you need enough storage to cover a cloudy day. The general rule is 1.5 times your daily critical load in watt-hours. Use our how to size a home battery walkthrough to calculate your own number. None of these kits will run a 4-ton central air conditioner, so set expectations before ordering. A window unit and refrigerator are realistic targets.

 Frequently Asked Questions # 
 What size off-grid solar kit do I need? 
 Add the running watts of every appliance you want to power. Multiply by 1.2 for surge. Then calculate daily watt-hours. A refrigerator and lights need 2,000W continuous and 4,000Wh storage. A well pump or furnace needs more surge headroom.
 Can an off-grid solar kit power a well pump? 
 Yes if the surge rating covers the pump’s locked rotor amps. A 1,800W well pump can need 3,600W to 5,400W for one second. Choose a kit with at least 6,000W surge.
 Do I need a permit for an off-grid solar kit? 
 Permanent rooftop arrays usually require a building and electrical permit. Portable kits that plug into a transfer switch may not need a roof permit. Check with your local authority before installing.
 How long do off-grid solar batteries last? 
 LFP batteries typically last 3,000 to 6,000 cycles to 80% capacity. That is 10 to 15 years under daily cycling. Temperature extremes and constant full discharges shorten life.
 Can I use an off-grid kit with a generator? 
 Yes. Many kits accept a generator input through an AC charger or a transfer switch. This gives you a backup for cloudy weeks without oversizing the solar array. Use a CO detector with any fuel generator.
 Does the federal solar tax credit apply to off-grid kits? 
 Yes if the system is installed at a residence, charges from solar, and you own the equipment. The credit is 30% through 2032 under current law. Consult a tax professional.
 What Should You Remember? # 
 Continuous output is the first spec to check. Match it to your largest simultaneous loads.
 Surge watts must cover motor starts. A well pump can require three times its running watts for a second.
 Usable storage should cover at least 1.5 times your daily critical load in watt-hours.
 Solar input determines recharge speed. More panel wattage means fewer cloudy-day gaps.
 Code compliance is non-negotiable. Hire a licensed electrician for any hardwired transfer switch.
 Battery chemistry matters. LFP lasts longer than older NMC under daily cycling.
